questions.stem: Which three substances are heated together in the flask?

options.text: Ethanoic acid, ethanol and concentrated sulfuric acid
options.explanation: The two parents plus the acid catalyst are the charged mixture.
Water is the product to be avoided, not an ingredient of the charge.

options.text: Ethanol, sodium carbonate and calcium chloride
options.explanation: Those two solutions belong to the purification stage afterwards.
Magnesium belongs to acid-metal reactions, not to this ester practical.

questions.stem: Why is a Bunsen burner not used for the heating?

options.text: Ethanol is flammable, so a naked flame is unsafe
options.explanation: A water bath or electric heater gives gentle heat without ignition risk.

options.text: The ester would burn away to nothing
options.explanation: The concern is igniting the ethanol vapour, not destroying the product.

options.text: The catalyst only works when cold
options.explanation: The method explicitly heats the mixture; only the heat source changes.

options.text: Bunsen flames are banned in all school practicals
options.explanation: Flames are used where safe; here the flammable ethanol rules one out.

questions.stem: Why is the ester distilled off as soon as it forms?

options.text: Removing it stops the reverse reaction turning it back into reactants
options.explanation: Taking the product away shifts the reaction in its favour and protects the yield.

options.text: To make its smell stronger in the sample
options.explanation: The distillation protects the yield; the smell is only a later check.

options.text: To save heating time and electricity
options.explanation: Economy is not the chemical reason; the reverse reaction is.

options.text: To keep the ester dissolved in the acid
options.explanation: The opposite is true: the method removes it from the mixture entirely.

questions.stem: Why do esters leave the reaction mixture before the other liquids?

options.text: Their low boiling points make them the first to evaporate
options.explanation: Volatility puts the ester at the front of the queue when the mixture warms.

options.text: They are the heaviest liquids present
options.explanation: Low boiling points, not heavy mass, decide who leaves first.

options.text: They are solids that melt early
options.explanation: Esters here are oily liquids from the start.
Water is the by-product and plays no part in the exit order.

questions.stem: How is the distilled ester collected?

options.text: In a separate beaker by condensation
options.explanation: The vapour cools back to liquid and gathers in its own vessel.
Filtration is for solids, and the ester arrives as a liquid.
The point of distilling off is to leave the flask behind.
No freezing stage exists in this method.

questions.stem: State the catalyst used in the flask when preparing ethyl ethanoate.
questions.modelAnswer: Concentrated sulfuric acid is the catalyst added to the ethanoic acid and ethanol.

questions.stem: How is the ester separated from the reaction mixture as it forms?
questions.modelAnswer: The ester is distilled off as soon as it forms and collected by condensation.

questions.stem: Explain why distilling the ester away as it forms raises the amount of ester finally made.
questions.modelAnswer: Removing the ester stops the reverse reaction from turning it back into the reactants, so more ester accumulates.

questions.stem: A student proposes heating the flask with a Bunsen burner to speed the reaction up. State the hazard that rules this out and the safer equipment to use instead.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethanol is flammable, so a naked Bunsen flame risks ignition; a water bath or electric heater is the safer choice.

questions.stem: How is the product checked before any washing begins?

options.explanation: The sweet smell of the ester is the quick qualitative check the method names.
Laboratory chemicals are never tasted, whatever they smell like.

options.text: By burning a little of it
options.explanation: Igniting a flammable distillate is not part of this method.
Mass alone cannot confirm which substances are present.

questions.stem: Why is sodium carbonate solution added to the distillate?

options.explanation: The carbonate neutralises both acids until none remain to fizz.

options.text: To add flavour to the ester
options.explanation: Flavouring happens in food factories, not in this purification.
Drying agents are different substances; the carbonate targets acids.
The reaction is already over; the carbonate works on impurities.

questions.stem: What is the fizzing during the sodium carbonate wash?

options.text: Carbon dioxide released as the carbonate meets the acids
options.explanation: Carbonate plus acid always releases the gas, and the fizzing shows it leaving.
No hydrogen is produced by this neutralisation.
Oxygen is not generated in an acid-carbonate reaction.
The distillate is already liquid; the bubbles are gas from the neutralisation.

questions.stem: What does the calcium chloride solution remove?

options.explanation: Calcium chloride is the named remover of ethanol from the sample.
The acids were already removed by the sodium carbonate wash.
Water removal is not the stated job of this solution here.
The product is what the washing is protecting, not removing.

questions.stem: Which contaminants can still be present in the raw distillate before washing?

options.text: Ethanoic acid, sulfuric acid and ethanol
options.explanation: All three travel over with the volatile ester during the distillation.
The method names three specific travellers, not just water.
Neither metal nor its gas plays any part in this practical.
No chloride salts are involved before the washing stage.

questions.stem: State the solution used to wash the acidic impurities out of the crude ester sample.
questions.modelAnswer: Sodium carbonate solution removes the acidic impurities from the distillate.

questions.stem: Which wash removes the leftover ethanol from the ester sample?
questions.modelAnswer: Calcium chloride solution removes the leftover ethanol.

questions.stem: Explain what the fizzing during the sodium carbonate wash tells you, and why it eventually stops.
questions.modelAnswer: The fizzing is carbon dioxide escaping as the carbonate neutralises the acid impurities; it stops when no acid remains to react.

questions.stem: After washing, a student waves a hand over the purified sample and notices a sweet, fruity smell. State what this observation confirms and name the class of compound present.
questions.modelAnswer: The sweet smell confirms that an ester has formed — the sample contains ethyl ethanoate.
